senses confused with ''blazon'', q. v.] '''1†.''' To blow, as from a trumpet.
{{smaller block|<poem>With his blake clarioun
He gan to ''blasen'' out a soun
As lowde as beloweth wynde in helle.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1802.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' To publish; make well known; announce in a public manner.
{{smaller block|<poem>Till we can find a time
To ''blaze'' your marriage. ''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 3.</poem>
To tell you truth, lady, his conceit was far better than I have ''blazed'' it yet.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, ii. 2.}}
<poem>Such musick worthiest were to ''blaze''
The peerless highth of her immortal praise.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Arcades, i. 74.}}}}
'''3†.''' To disclose; betray; defame.
{{smaller block|<poem>To cover shame, I took thee; never fear
That I would ''blaze'' myself.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, ii. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' In ''her.'', to blazon. See ''blazon'', ''n.'', 1 and 2.
{{smaller block|You should have ''blazed'' it thus: he bears a tierce sable between two tierces or. {{right|''Peacham.''}}
<poem>Braggadochio . . . did shew his shield,
Which bore the Sunne brode ''blazed'' in a golden field.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. iii. 14.}}}}

'''blaze'''<sup>2</sup> (blāz), ''n.'' [< ''blaze''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] Publication; the act of spreading widely by report. [Poetic.]
{{smaller block|For what is glory but the ''blaze'' of fame?
{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iii. 47.}}}}

'''blaze'''<sup>3</sup> (blāz), ''n.'' [= D. ''bles'' = MLG. ''blesse'' = MHG. ''blasse'', G. ''blässe'' = Icel. ''blesi'' = Sw. ''bläs''

''blass'', pale, wan, orig. ‘shining’; connected with ''blaze''<sup>1</sup>, a torch, flame: see ''blaze''<sup>1</sup>; cf. Icel. ''blasa'', lie open to view.] '''1.''' A white spot on the face of a horse, cow, ox, etc. See cut under ''blesbok''.
{{smaller block|A square ''blaze'' in his [a sacred ox’s] forehead.
{{right|''Cowley'', Plagues of Egypt, note to st. 16.}}}}
'''2.''' A white mark made on a tree, as by removing a piece of the bark, to indicate a boundary, or a path or trail in a forest. [Orig. American.] —'''3.''' A local English name of the bleak.

¶
'''blaze'''<sup>3</sup> (blāz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''blazed'', ppr. ''blazing''. [= MLG. ''blesset'', pp.; < ''blaze''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.''] '''1.''' To mark with a white spot on the face, as a horse: only in the perfect participle ''blazed''.—'''2.''' To set a mark on, as a tree, usually by cutting off a piece of its bark, so as to show a white spot.
{{smaller block|As for me, the son and the father of Uncas, I am a ''blazed'' pine in the clearing of the pale-faces.
{{right|''Cooper'', Last of Mohicans, xxxiii.}}}}
'''3.''' To indicate or mark out, as by cutting off pieces of the bark of a number of trees in succession: as, to ''blaze'' a path through a forest.
{{smaller block|Champollion died in 1832, having done little more than ''blaze'' out the road to be traveled by others. {{right|''Nott.''}}}}

¶
'''blaze'''<sup>5</sup> (blāz), ''n.'' [Origin uncertain.] Same as ''brash''<sup>1</sup>, 4 (''a'').

'''blaze'''<sup>6</sup> (blāz), ''n. pl.'' Irregular spelling of ''blaes'', plural of ''blae''. See ''blae'', ''n.''

'''blazer'''<sup>1</sup> (blā′zėr), ''n.'' [< ''blaze''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Anything that blazes, or is intensely luminous or hot: as, the day was a ''blazer''.—'''2.''' A dish under which there is a receptacle for coals to keep it hot.—'''3.''' A bright-colored loose coat, usually of flannel, worn by tennis- and cricket-players.
{{smaller block|The origin of the word is as follows: The uniform of the Lady Margaret Boat Club of St. John’s College, Cambridge, is bright red, and the Johnian jackets have for many years been called ''blazers''. Up to a few years ago the inaccurate modern use of ''blazer'' for a jacket of any other colour than red was unknown.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., III. 436.}}}}

'''blazer'''<sup>2</sup> (blā′zėr), ''n.'' [< ''blaze''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who blazes; one who publishes and spreads reports: as, “''blazers'' of cryme,” ''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ix. 25.—'''2†.''' A blazoner.

'''blazer'''<sup>3</sup> (blā′zėr), ''n.'' [< ''blaze''<sup>3</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who blazes a tree.

'''blazingly''' (blā′zing-li), ''adv.'' In a blazing manner.

'''blazing-star''' (blā′zing-stär′), ''n.'' '''1.''' In ''her.'', a comet used as a bearing. {{smaller|It is represented bendwise as a star of six points with a tail streaming from it.}} '''2.''' A name in the United States for several very different plants. {{smaller|(''a'') The ''Aletris farinosa'', a low herbaceous plant, natural order ''Hæmodoraceæ'', with whitish mealy flowers. The roots are bitter, and have some repute in medicine. Also called ''colic-root''. (''b'') The}}

'''blazy''' (blā′zi), ''a.'' [< ''blaze''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Burning brightly; blazing: as, a ''blazy'' fire. [Rare.]

'''ble†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''blee.''

'''-ble.''' [ME. ''-ble'' (''-bel'', ''-bil'', ''-byl'', ''-bul''), < OF. ''-ble'', mod. F. ''-ble'' = Pr. Sp. ''-ble'' = Pg. ''-vel'' = It. ''-bile'', < L. ''-bilis'', acc. ''-bilem'', a suffix (< ''-bi-'' + ''-li-s''), forming adjectives, usually with a passive signification, from verbs ending with one of the vowels ''-ā'', ''-ē'', ''-ī'', ''-ĭ'', ''-ō'', ''-ū'', being the root- or stem-vowel or (as usually ''-ĭ'') a mere insertion, as in ''admirā-bilis'', ''delē-bilis'', ''sepelī-bilis'', ''cred-ĭ-bilis'', ''ignō-bilis'', ''mō-bilis'', ''volū-bilis'', etc.; rarely from perfect participles, as in ''flex-ĭ-bilis'', ''plaus-ĭ-bilis'', etc. See further under ''-able.'' Adjectives in ''-ble'' are accompanied by adverbs in ''-bly'', contr. from ''-ble-ly'', and nouns in ''-ble-ness'' or, according to the L., in ''-bil-ity'', as ''credi-ble'', ''credi-bleness'', ''credi-bility.'' In many words the term. ''-ble'' is of different origin, as in ''nimble'', ''hamble'', ''humble'', ''marble'', ''parable'', ''syllable'', etc., divided etymologically ''nimb-le'', ''humb-le'', etc., the real term. being ''-le'', of various origin.] A suffix of Latin origin, occurring in adjectives having originally a passive signification, which is retained more or less fully in adjectives accompanied by verbs derived from the infinitive or perfect participle (English ''-ate'' or ''-it'') of the same Latin verb, as in ''commendable'', ''admirable'', ''dissoluble'', etc., ''habitable'', ''imitable'', ''tolerable'', ''navi-''
readings.c3s2:
gable'', etc., ''credible'', etc., but is not obvious in adjectives not accompanied by such verbs, as in ''equable'', ''delectable'', ''horrible'', ''terrible'', ''ignoble'', ''voluble'', ''feeble'', etc. In English it is felt and used as a suffix only with the preceding vowel, ''-able'' or ''-ible''. See ''-able'', ''-ible''.

¶
'''blea'''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'' and ''n.'' See ''blae''.

'''blea'''<sup>2</sup> (blē), ''n.'' [Origin uncertain; perhaps < ''blea''<sup>1</sup> = ''blae'', pale (see ''blae''). Cf. Sc. ''blae'', ''blay'', rough parts of wood left in sawing or boring.] The part of a tree immediately under the bark; the alburnum or white wood. [Rare.]

'''bleaberry''', ''n.'' Same as ''blaeberry''.

'''bleach'''<sup>1</sup> (blēch), ''v.'' [< ME. ''blechen'', < AS. ''blǣcan'' (= D. ''bleeken'' = OHG. ''bleichēn'', MHG. G. ''bleichen'' = Icel. ''bleikja'' = Sw. ''bleka'' = Dan. ''blege''), make white, cause to fade (cf. ''blācian'', become white or pale), < ''blāc'', pale, bleak: see ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>, ''blake''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To make white or whiter by removing color; whiten; blanch; make pale; specifically, to whiten (as linen, etc.) by washing and exposure to the action of the air and sunlight, or by chemical preparations. See ''bleaching''.
{{smaller block|Immortal liberty, whose look sublime
Hath ''bleached'' the tyrant’s cheek in every varying clime.
{{right|''Smollett'', Ode to Independence.}}
<poem>The bones of men,
In some forgotten battle slain,
And ''bleached'' by drifting wind and rain.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iii. 5.}}
The robed and mitred apostles, ''bleached'' and rain-washed by the ages, rose into the blue air like huge snow figures.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 210.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Blanch'', etc. See ''whiten''.

¶ '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To become white in any manner; become pale or colorless. {{smaller block|Along the snows a stiffened corse,
Stretched out and ''bleaching'' in the northern blast. {{right|''Thomson'', Winter, l. 321.}}}} '''2.''' To become morally pure. [Rare.] '''bleach1†''', ''a.'' [< ME. ''bleche'' (''blēche''), < AS. ''blǣc'', var. of ''blāc'', pale: see ''bleak''1, ''blake'', and cf. ''bleach''1, ''v.''] '''1.''' Pale.—'''2.''' Bleak. '''bleach1''' (blēch), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bleche'', < AS. ''blǣco'', paleness, < ''blāc'', pale: see ''bleak''1.] '''1†.''' A disease of the skin. ''Holland'', tr. of Pliny.—'''2.''' [< ''bleach''1, ''v.''] An act of bleaching; exposure to the sun or other bleaching agency or influence. {{smaller block|What is known as “the three-quarter ''bleach''” with flax. {{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LVI. 249.}}}} '''bleach2†''' (blēch), ''n.'' [A var. of ''bletch'', q. v.] Blacking; any substance used for blacking. ''Cotgrave.'' '''bleacher''' (blē′chėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who bleaches; one whose occupation is to whiten cloth.—'''2.''' A vessel used in bleaching.—'''3.''' A large shallow wooden tub, lined with metal, used in distilling petroleum; a settling-tub. '''bleachery''' (blē′chėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''bleacheries'' (-iz). [< ''bleach''1, ''v.'', + ''-ery''.] A place for bleaching; an establishment where the bleaching of textile fabrics, etc., is carried on. {{smaller block|Young reprobates dyed in the wool with perversity are taken into a kind of moral ''bleachery'' and come out white as lambs. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Old Vol. of Life, p. 354.}}}} '''bleach-field''' (blēch′fēld), ''n.'' A field where cloth or yarn is bleached.

'''blazingly''' (blā′zing-li), ''adv.'' In a blazing manner.

'''blazing-star''' (blā′zing-stär′), ''n.'' '''1.''' In ''her.'', a comet used as a bearing. {{smaller|It is represented bendwise as a star of six points with a tail streaming from it.}} '''2.''' A name in the United States for several very different plants. {{smaller|(''a'') The ''Aletris farinosa'', a low herbaceous plant, natural order ''Hæmodoraceæ'', with whitish mealy flowers. The roots are bitter, and have some repute in medicine. Also called ''colic-root''. (''b'') The starwort (''Chamælirium Carolinianum''), natural order ''Liliaceæ'', the roots of which yield a bitter tonic. (''c'') A species of ''Liatris'', ''L. squarrosa'', natural order ''Compositæ'', one of the many popular remedies for rattlesnake-bites.}}
'''3.''' A stampede of pack-mules or other animals from a central point. [Western U. S. slang.]

'''blazon''' (blā′zn), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blason'', ''blasoun'', a shield, = MD. ''blasoen'', D. ''blazoen'', < OF. ''blason'', ''blazon'' (= Pr. ''blezo'', ''blizo'' = Sp. ''blason'' = Pg. ''blasão'', ''brasão'' = It. ''blasone''), a shield with a coat of arms painted on it, the coat of arms itself (the Pr. and Sp. terms mean also honor, glory, fame); usually referred to MHG. ''blāsen'', OHG. ''blāsan'', blow, hence sound a trumpet, proclaim, blaze (see ''blaze''<sup>2</sup>); by some to ''blaze''<sup>1</sup>; but the orig. sense ‘shield,’ with other facts, is against such derivation. In ME. and mod. E. ''blaze''<sup>2</sup> and ''blazon'' are of course associated in thought.]   '''1.''' In ''her.'', a shield with arms on it; armorial bearings; a coat of arms; a banner bearing arms.
{{smaller block|The chief functionaries of city and province, . . . all marching under emblematical standards or time-honored ''blazons''.
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, III. 533.}}}}
'''2.''' A description in technical language of armorial bearings. {{smaller|Peculiar and fantastic changes introduced by certain heralds are chiefly in the blazon, and not in the graphic representation: thus, when the arms of nobles are described by precious stones (sapphire instead of azure, topaz instead of or, and the like), or when the arms of sovereigns are described by the planets, the description only is peculiar, the drawing and coloring of the achievement being of the same character as those of ordinary bearings.}}
'''3†.''' Interpretation; explanation.
{{smaller block|I think your ''blazon'' to be true. {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1.}}}}
<poem>But this eternal ''blazon'' must not be
To ears of flesh and blood.   ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 5.</poem>

'''blazon''' (blā′zn), ''v. t.''   [= MD. ''blasoenen'' = G. ''blasoniren'', < F. ''blasonner'', blazon, = Sp. ''blasonar'', blazon, brag, boast, = It. ''blasonare'', blazon (ML. ''blazonare''); from the noun. Cf. ''blaze''<sup>2</sup> in similar senses.]   '''1.''' To explain in proper heraldic terms (the arms or bearings on a shield).
{{smaller block|King Edward gave to them the coat of arms which I am not herald enough to ''blazon'' into English. {{right|''Addison.''}}}}
'''2.''' To depict (armorial bearings) according to the rules of heraldry. [An incorrect use of the word, not recognized by heralds.]—'''3.''' To inscribe with arms, or some ornament; adorn with blazonry.
{{smaller block|The blood-red flag of the Sacred Office . . . ''blazoned'' upon either side with the portraits of Alexander and of Ferdinand. {{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, II. iii. 166.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What matter whose the hillside grave,
Or whose the ''blazoned'' stone?</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Countess.}}}}
'''4.''' To deck; embellish; adorn as with blazonry.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then ''blazons'' in dread smiles her hideous form.</poem>
{{right|''Garth'', The Dispensary, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The bottom of the valley was a bed of glorious grass, ''blazoned'' with flowers.
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Lands of the Saracen, p. 280.}}}}
'''5.''' To display; exhibit conspicuously; make known; publish.
{{smaller block|<poem>For better farre it were to hide their names,</poem> Than telling them to ''blazon'' out their blames.
{{right|''Spenser'', Teares of the Muses.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Blazoning'' our injustice everywhere.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|And ''blazon'' o’er the door their names in brass.
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, xi. 31.}}}}
'''6.''' To proclaim or publish boastingly; boast of.
{{smaller block|My friend Lancelot is not a man to ''blazon'' anything.
{{right|''Irving'', Salmagundi, p. 124.}}}}

'''blazoner''' (blā′zn-ėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who blazons; a herald.—'''2.''' One who publishes or proclaims with strong or extravagant praise.

'''blazoning''' (blā′zn-ing), ''n.'' In ''her.'', the art of describing armorial bearings. See ''blazon, n.''

'''blazonment''' (blā′zn-ment), ''n.''   [< ''blazon'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of blazoning; emblazonment.

'''blazonry''' (blā′zn-ri), ''n.''   [< ''blazon'' + ''-ry.'']   '''1.''' The art of describing or explaining coats of arms in proper heraldic terms and method.
{{smaller block|Bob has done more to set the public right on this important point of ''blazonry'' than the whole College of Heralds. {{right|''Lamb'', Newspapers Thirty-five Years ago.}}}}
'''2.''' Emblazonry; decoration in color, as with heraldic devices; brilliant decoration; splendor.
{{smaller block|The gorgeous building and wild ''blazonry'' of that shrine of St. Mark’s. {{right|''Ruskin.''}}}}
{{smaller block|So much subtler is a human mind than the outside tissues which make a sort of ''blazonry'' or clockface for it.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, I. 12.}}}}
'''3.''' Figuratively, display.

'''blazy''' (blā′zi), ''a.''   [< ''blaze''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Burning brightly; blazing: as, a ''blazy'' fire. [Rare.]

'''ble†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''blee.''

'''-ble.'''   [ME. ''-ble'' (''-bel'', ''-bil'', ''-byl'', ''-bul''), < OF. ''-ble'', mod. F. ''-ble'' = Pr. Sp. ''-ble'' = Pg. ''-vel'' = It. ''-bile'', < L. ''-bilis'', acc. ''-bilem'', a suffix (< ''-bi-'' + ''-li-s''), forming adjectives, usually with a passive signification, from verbs ending with one of the vowels ''-ā'', ''-ē'', ''-ī'', ''-ĭ'', ''-ō'', ''-ū'', being the root- or stem-vowel or (as usually ''-ĭ'') a mere insertion, as in ''admirā-bilis'', ''delē-bilis'', ''sepelī-bilis'', ''cred-ĭ-bilis'', ''ignō-bilis'', ''mō-bilis'', ''volū-bilis'', etc.; rarely from perfect participles, as in ''flex-ĭ-bilis'', ''plaus-ĭ-bilis'', etc. See further under ''-able.'' Adjectives in ''-ble'' are accompanied by adverbs in ''-bly'', contr. from ''-ble-ly'', and nouns in ''-ble-ness'' or, according to the L., in ''-bil-ity'', as ''credi-ble'', ''credi-bleness'', ''credi-bility.'' In many words the term. ''-ble'' is of different origin, as in ''nimble'', ''hamble'', ''humble'', ''marble'', ''parable'', ''syllable'', etc., divided etymologically ''nimb-le'', ''humb-le'', etc., the real term. being ''-le'', of various origin.]   A suffix of Latin origin, occurring in adjectives having originally a passive signification, which is retained more or less fully in adjectives accompanied by verbs derived from the infinitive or perfect participle (English ''-ate'' or ''-it'') of the same Latin verb, as in ''commendable'', ''admirable'', ''dissoluble'', etc., ''habitable'', ''imitable'', ''tolerable'', ''navigable'''', etc., ''credible'', etc., but is not obvious in adjectives not accompanied by such verbs, as in ''equable'', ''delectable'', ''horrible'', ''terrible'', ''ignoble'', ''voluble'', ''feeble'', etc. In English it is felt and used as a suffix only with the preceding vowel, ''-able'' or ''-ible''. See ''-able'', ''-ible''.

'''blea'''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'' and ''n.'' See ''blae''.

'''blea'''<sup>2</sup> (blē), ''n.''   [Origin uncertain; perhaps < ''blea''<sup>1</sup> = ''blae'', pale (see ''blae''). Cf. Sc. ''blae'', ''blay'', rough parts of wood left in sawing or boring.]   The part of a tree immediately under the bark; the alburnum or white wood. [Rare.]

'''bleaberry''', ''n.'' Same as ''blaeberry''.

'''bleach'''<sup>1</sup> (blēch), ''v.''   [< ME. ''blechen'', < AS. ''blǣcan'' (= D. ''bleeken'' = OHG. ''bleichēn'', MHG. G. ''bleichen'' = Icel. ''bleikja'' = Sw. ''bleka'' = Dan. ''blege''), make white, cause to fade (cf. ''blācian'', become white or pale), < ''blāc'', pale, bleak: see ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>, ''blake''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To make white or whiter by removing color; whiten; blanch; make pale; specifically, to whiten (as linen, etc.) by washing and exposure to the action of the air and sunlight, or by chemical preparations. See ''bleaching''.
{{smaller block|Immortal liberty, whose look sublime
Hath ''bleached'' the tyrant’s cheek in every varying clime.
{{right|''Smollett'', Ode to Independence.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The bones of men,
In some forgotten battle slain,
And ''bleached'' by drifting wind and rain.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|The robed and mitred apostles, ''bleached'' and rain-washed by the ages, rose into the blue air like huge snow figures.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 210.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Blanch'', etc. See ''whiten''.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To become white in any manner; become pale or colorless.
{{smaller block|<poem>Along the snows a stiffened corse,
Stretched out and ''bleaching'' in the northern blast.</poem>
{{right|''Thomson'', Winter, l. 321.}}}}
'''2.''' To become morally pure. [Rare.]

'''bleach<sup>1</sup>†''', ''a.''   [< ME. ''bleche'' (''blēche''), < AS. ''blǣc'', var. of ''blāc'', pale: see ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>, ''blake'', and cf. ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' Pale.—'''2.''' Bleak.

'''bleach<sup>1</sup>''' (blēch), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bleche'', < AS. ''blǣco'', paleness, < ''blāc'', pale: see ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' A disease of the skin.   ''Holland'', tr. of Pliny.—'''2.''' [< ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] An act of bleaching; exposure to the sun or other bleaching agency or influence.
{{smaller block|What is known as “the three-quarter ''bleach''” with flax.
{{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LVI. 249.}}}}

'''bleach<sup>2</sup>†''' (blēch), ''n.''   [A var. of ''bletch'', q. v.]   Blacking; any substance used for blacking.   ''Cotgrave.''

'''bleacher''' (blē′chėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who bleaches; one whose occupation is to whiten cloth.—'''2.''' A vessel used in bleaching.—'''3.''' A large shallow wooden tub, lined with metal, used in distilling petroleum; a settling-tub.

'''bleachery''' (blē′chėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''bleacheries'' (-iz).   [< ''bleach''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-ery''.]   A place for bleaching; an establishment where the bleaching of textile fabrics, etc., is carried on.
{{smaller block|Young reprobates dyed in the wool with perversity are taken into a kind of moral ''bleachery'' and come out white as lambs. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Old Vol. of Life, p. 354.}}}}

'''bleach-field''' (blēch′fēld), ''n.'' A field where cloth or yarn is bleached.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
